title: Гладиатор в чужой спальне  (A Gladiator in the Wrong Bedroom)

segments.t: Dressed in a Roman gladiator helmet and cape, Barinov leaps onto the bed in suite 311—only to come face to face with Eleonora! Terrified that Elena in the adjoining room will hear them, Victor begs Eleonora to leave and tells Elena it was just a maid.
Кто здесь
заказывал сегодня
шефа в номер на всю...
Витя, черт.
Что здесь делаешь? Я? Я собираюсь спать.
А теперь собирайся и уходи отсюда.
Пожалуйста, умоляю тебя.
В этом номере другая женщина.
Я не хочу, чтобы она тебя видела. Витя, это ты?
Умоляю, не губи мою жизнь снова.
Завтра, завтра можешь меня уволить.
С кем ты тут разговаривал?
А горничная заходила, я ей сказал, что у тебя уже есть горничная.
Бред какой-то.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
Кто здесь
'Who in here' Barinov sustains a direct line for Elena, pairing "zdes" ("here") with "kto" ("who") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
заказывал сегодня
'ordered tonight' Barinov adopts an emphatic mood across the room, weaving "zakazyval" ("ordered") together with "segodnya" ("today") just the way native speakers do.
шефа в номер на всю...
'the Chef to the room for the whole...' Barinov takes an easygoing angle on the spot, using "shefa" (from "shef", "chef") alongside "nomer" ("number") to shape the meaning.
Витя, черт.
'Vitya, damn it!' Eleonora keeps a measured stance in front of Elena, building the phrase around "chert" ("darn, heck") and "vitya" ("Vitya") for a crisp, natural delivery.
Что здесь делаешь? Я? Я собираюсь спать.
'What are you doing here? Me? I am getting ready to sleep.' Barinov asks sharply on the spot, putting "zdes" ("here") alongside "delayesh" ("are you doing") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
А теперь собирайся и уходи отсюда.

'And now pack up and get out of here.' Barinov maintains an earnest posture as the scene unfolds, pairing "sobiraysya" ("gather yourself") with "teper" ("now") so the "-sya" ending carries the action.
Пожалуйста, умоляю тебя.
'Please, I beg you.' Barinov sustains a lively posture in the scene, joining "umolyayu" ("I beg") to "pozhaluysta" ("please") so every word pulls its weight.
В этом номере другая женщина.
'There is another woman in this suite.' Barinov picks a direct view with Eleonora, leaning on "nomere" ("in the hotel room") before closing the thought with "drugaya" ("different, other").
Я не хочу, чтобы она тебя видела. Витя, это ты?
'I do not want her to see you. Vitya, is that you?' Eleonora challenges firmly beside Barinov, using "khochu" (from "khotet", "want") alongside "videla" ("saw") to shape the meaning.
Умоляю, не губи мою жизнь снова.
'I beg you, do not ruin my life again.' Barinov conveys a thoughtful angle on the spot, using "umolyayu" (from "umolyat", "I beg") alongside "gubi" ("ruin, destroy") to shape the meaning.
Завтра, завтра можешь меня уволить.
'Tomorrow, you can fire me tomorrow.' Barinov picks a playful tempo toward Elena, leaning on "zavtra" ("tomorrow") before closing the thought with "mozhesh" ("can").
С кем ты тут разговаривал?
'Who were you talking to in here?' Elena challenges calmly without holding back, linking "tut" ("here"), "razgovarival" ("spoke, talked"), and "kem" ("as what") in one brisk exchange.
А горничная заходила, я ей сказал, что у тебя уже есть горничная.

'Oh, a maid came in, and I told her you already have a maid.' Barinov adopts a measured course at this moment, combining "u tebya" (literally "by you") with "gornichnaya" ("maid") rather than a separate word for "have".
Бред какой-то.
'Some kind of nonsense.' Elena establishes a measured attitude in the conversation, combining "bred" ("nonsense") and "kakoy-to" ("some") so the key meaning lands right away.
